after.authors: Raut, S.; Hales, A.; Yates, D.; Danjoux, G.; Ingle, L.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Hull University Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust
after.abstract: Introduction: The average waiting time for urgent coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) is 13 days in England and Wales and 27 days in Northern Ireland; significantly longer than the National Institute for Cardiovascular Outcomes Research (NICOR) recommendation of 7 days.Inpatients are at risk of Hospital-Associated Deconditioning (HAD) which impacts cognitive and physical function, increases mortality and healthcare cost. Prehabilitation has been shown to improve physical function and reduce complications in the elective population. Prehabilitation has never been attempted in acute inpatients waiting for cardiac surgery.   Methods: Participants were recruited between April 2024 and February 2025. Once consented, the participants were provided with psychoeducation booklet and underwent assessments; 6 minute walk test (6MWT), hand grip test (HGT), spirometry, EQ-5D-5L and cardiac anxiety questionnaire (CAQ) on day 0, 7 and 14. The physiotherapy team assessed and prescribed personalised exercise. Information regarding their in-hospital stay were collected. Our primary outcome was determining the feasibility of prehabilitation. The secondary outcome was to identify any adverse events related to the intervention and changes in the assessment results. The PreP-ACe trial was ethically approved by the Health Research Authority and Health and Care Research Wales (Yorkshire & the Humber- Bradford Leeds Research Ethics Committee: REC reference 23/YH/0255) on the 8th November 2023. Results: 17 participants were recruited resulting in a recruitment rate of 1.5 participants per month. 1 participant withdrew from the study. 7 participants were seen by physiotherapist and participated in the exercise program. The adherence to the exercise program was 100% with tolerability of >80%. No adverse events related to exercise recorded. 11 participants remained in the study for 7 days or more.         Discussion: Prehabilitation is a novel concept of preparing inpatients for acute cardiac surgery. There are several challenges in determining the feasibility of prehabilitation in this population. These include identifying the best time to recruit, optimal level of exercise, funding (staffing to execute the intervention) and clinician reception towards the intervention. However, prehabilitation was well accepted, tolerated and adhered to by participants.

after.title: Preprint: Thoracic expansion and spirometry 120 days after adding diaphragmatic manual therapy to physiotherapy in non-specific low back pain: Follow-up of a randomized controlled trial
after.authors: Vera Serrano, F. J.; Vinolo-Gil, M. J.; Vera Serrano, P. A.; Gonzalez-Rubino, J. B.; Garcia-Campanario, I.; Diaz Mancha, J. A.
after.author_corresponding_institution: University of Cadiz: Universidad de Cadiz
after.abstract: Objective An interim analysis of the DIAFRAGMA trial (46 participants) found that adding manual diaphragmatic stretching to physiotherapy improved thoracic expansion, forced vital capacity and forced expiratory volume in one second up to 30 days in non-specific low back pain. We assessed whether these differences persist at 120 days and, exploratorily, whether baseline values moderate the response. Methods In this parallel-group, assessor-blinded randomized controlled trial, 55 adults were randomized and 50 were analysed (22 experimental, 28 control). All participants received ten sessions of conventional physiotherapy; the experimental group also received manual diaphragmatic stretching in six of them. Thoracic expansion (cirtometry at three levels) and portable spirometry were assessed at baseline, after the first and tenth sessions, and 7, 30 and 120 days after treatment. Between-group differences were estimated with linear mixed-effects models and false discovery rate correction. Results At 120 days, inspiratory thoracic expansion was greater in the experimental group at the axillary (3.38 cm; 95% CI 2.94 to 3.81), xiphoid (3.52 cm; 2.78 to 4.26) and basal levels (4.12 cm; 3.36 to 4.88). Forced vital capacity (1.57 L; 0.96 to 2.18), forced expiratory volume in one second (1.49 L; 0.97 to 2.01) and peak expiratory flow (2.70 L/s; 1.21 to 4.19) were also higher (all p < 0.001). These differences arose during treatment and remained stable thereafter. Expiratory-phase expansion and mid-to-late expiratory flows did not improve. No baseline value moderated the response. Conclusions Adding manual diaphragmatic stretching to physiotherapy was associated with greater inspiratory chest expansion and higher spirometric values that were maintained at 120 days. Because of the size of the spirometric differences, the portable spirometry protocol and the lack of participant blinding and a sham comparator, these findings require confirmation in sham-controlled trials using laboratory spirometry. Trial registration ClinicalTrials.gov NCT06069388.

after.title: Preprint: Transcriptomic and Genomic Sequencing of South African Colorectal Cancer Patients Reveal Population-Specific Insights and Variants
after.authors: Kader, Z.; Abdulla, N.; Bebington, B.; Choudhury, A.; Mpangase, P.; Kinnear, C.; Kaur, M.
after.abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) genomic studies have largely underrepresented African populations, limiting understanding of disease biology in these groups. This study addressed this gap by generating integrated genomic and transcriptomic data from South African (SA) CRC patients, establishing a foundation for future cancer studies. Bulk RNA sequencing of 32 samples identified several differentially expressed genes between tumour and normal samples, with AGAP3, AMPD2, ANKRD10, and SALL4 showing strong diagnostic performance (average sensitivity 99.9%, specificity 94.22%, PPV 99.9%, NPV 89.5%). SALL4 performed best and was validated using TCGA data and Kaplan-Meier survival analysis. Consensus Molecular Subtype classification revealed a distinct distribution, with enrichment of metabolic (CMS3, 30%) and mesenchymal (CMS4, 30%) subtypes and under-representation of canonical CMS2 (21%). APC mutation rates were lower than in European patients (~55% vs ~75%). Functional analysis identified inflammatory pathways as primary drivers of carcinogenesis, with viral influences exacerbating the inflammatory tumour microenvironment. Altered neural pathways in tumour samples suggested a consequential gut-brain axis loop as cancer infiltrates enervated tissue, an increasingly relevant field to which these data contribute. Whole-genome sequencing of 12 samples revealed pathogenic and likely pathogenic variants with transcriptomic differential expression; SMPD1, PERM1, PRRT2, and RP1 emerged as potential multi-omics markers, while novel mutations (KDM6A, C2CD2, TAF2, SLC6A16, OR5M10, PITRM1, TRIM64B, CARD11) were identified as previously unrecognised contributors to CRC progression in African samples. These findings expand genomic resources for African cancer research and provide new insights into the molecular landscape and tumourigenesis mechanisms of CRC in SA patients, supporting the development of population-specific precision oncology approaches.

after.title: Preprint: A new liability-based rare-variant burden test identifies a novel genetic association between HTRA3 and idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis
after.authors: Chun, S.; Samiei, A.; Flynn, L.; Makrynioti, H.; Moll, M.; Peljto, A. L.; Schwartz, D. A.; Cho, M. H.; Sunyaev, S. R.; Rosas, I. O.; Hunninghake, G. M.; Raby, B. A.
after.abstract: In contrast to large-effect monogenic variants, which are highly penetrant regardless of genetic background, variants with more modest effect sizes depend on a carrier's genetic background to manifest disease. For many complex traits, including idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF), polygenic risk scores (PRS) have been shown to capture a significant proportion of the genetic background risk. While a rare-variant association test incorporating a PRS covariate to account for the genetic background has been demonstrated to improve statistical power for gene discovery in quantitative traits, for binary traits, this approach shows limited or no power gain over PRS-unadjusted tests. Here, we propose a novel rare-variant association test for binary traits that jointly models the contribution of rare variants and PRS under a liability threshold model. In simulated datasets, our new method, liability threshold burden test (LTBT), shows a well-controlled false positive rate and outperforms the sensitivity of existing methods. To demonstrate this new method, we apply it to sequencing datasets for IPF, a rare but highly morbid lung disease. By accounting for an individual's genetic background with PRS, we identify and formally replicate a significant novel association of rare predicted damaging missense variants in HTRA3 (HtrA serine peptidase 3) with IPF.

after.title: Preprint: Excess of de novo substitutions in the genomes of individuals with newly acquired germline TP53 mutations
after.authors: Parmentier, M.; Montierth, M. D.; Li, R.; Recio, C. V.; Chau, G. P.; Li, B.; Chen, R.; Lozano, G.; Tarabichi, M.; Wang, W.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Department of Bioinformatics and Computational Biology, The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center, Houston, TX, USA
after.abstract: Inherited defects in the tumour suppressor gene TP53 cause Li-Fraumeni syndrome, a highly penetrant predisposition to childhood and adult cancers. About half of affected individuals carry a variant absent from both parents, and these are the patients missed by family-history-based testing criteria. Where and when such variants arise, in which parental gamete or after fertilisation, remains unresolved, as primary family data are scarce. We addressed this using whole-genome and linked-read sequencing of five family quartets, each comprising a proband with a confirmed newly arisen pathogenic TP53 variant, a closely age-matched unaffected sibling, and both parents, drawn from a cohort of 429 families meeting clinical criteria for the syndrome; matching for age controls for the strong dependence of mutation counts on parental age. Every proband carried a distinct heterozygous missense change in the DNA-binding domain of p53, and read-based phasing traced four of five to the paternal chromosome. Genome-wide, probands carried a significant excess of newly arisen single-nucleotide changes relative to their siblings, which persisted after correction for parental age and was detected on the paternal chromosome. No comparable excess was found for insertions, deletions, structural rearrangements or repeat expansions, and the excess mutations matched the two clock-like processes operating in all cells rather than any distinct mechanism. These features are hard to reconcile with an event confined to the parental germ cells, and instead point to TP53 variants that arise shortly after fertilisation and sweep the embryo, carrying neighbouring mutations with them. Consistent with such sweeps occurring throughout life, TP53 mutations in two large public tumour-genome collections were more clonal than other driver mutations, and the most clonal were present in more cells than the tumour itself, as expected when a cancer emerges within a pre-existing mutant patch of normal tissue. We propose that constitutional TP53 variants and these mutant patches form one continuum, distinguished principally by timing: a sweep during the first cleavage divisions produces a variant present throughout the body, whereas the same advantage acting later confines the clone to one tissue. This reframes a subset of Li-Fraumeni syndrome as an early developmental rather than strictly germline event, with implications for testing, counselling and surveillance.

About half of affected individuals carry a variant absent from both parents, and these are the patients missed by family-history-based testing criteria. Where and when such variants arise, in which parental gamete or after fertilisation, remains unresolved, as primary family data are scarce. We addressed this using whole-genome and linked-read sequencing of five family quartets, each comprising a proband with a confirmed newly arisen pathogenic TP53 variant, a closely age-matched unaffected sibling, and both parents, drawn from a cohort of 429 families meeting clinical criteria for the syndrome; matching for age controls for the strong dependence of mutation counts on parental age. Every proband carried a distinct heterozygous missense change in the DNA-binding domain of p53, and read-based phasing traced four of five to the paternal chromosome. Genome-wide, probands carried a significant excess of newly arisen single-nucleotide changes relative to their siblings, which persisted after correction for parental age and was detected on the paternal chromosome. No comparable excess was found for insertions, deletions, structural rearrangements or repeat expansions, and the excess mutations matched the two clock-like processes operating in all cells rather than any distinct mechanism. These features are hard to reconcile with an event confined to the parental germ cells, and instead point to TP53 variants that arise shortly after fertilisation and sweep the embryo, carrying neighbouring mutations with them. Consistent with such sweeps occurring throughout life, TP53 mutations in two large public tumour-genome collections were more clonal than other driver mutations, and the most clonal were present in more cells than the tumour itself, as expected when a cancer emerges within a pre-existing mutant patch of normal tissue. after.abstract: Missense variants in the DNA-binding domains of PAX9 and MSX1 cause non-syndromic tooth agenesis, yet most substitutions remain variants of uncertain significance. We investigated the structural mechanisms of 39 pathogenic missense variants in the PAX9 paired domain (n = 32) and MSX1 homeodomain (n = 7) alongside 77 non-coding/splice ClinVar variants. We modelled protein-DNA complexes with AlphaFold 3, estimated folding stability changes ({Delta}{Delta}G) with ThermoMPNN, and compared pathogenic variants with gnomAD v4 domain variants. AlphaFold 3 confidence metrics and mutant interfaces were insensitive to point mutations. Instead, pathogenic PAX9 variants acted through two complementary mechanisms relative to recurrent population controls: loss of direct DNA contact (< 4 [A]; 50% vs 17%; p = 0.0025) or domain destabilization (median {Delta}{Delta}G 1.17 vs 0.34 kcal/mol; p = 4.6x10-5). Leave-one-out cross-validation selected a stable rule (DNA contact or {Delta}{Delta}G [≥] 1.5 kcal/mol; apparent sensitivity 84%, specificity 79%) concordant with published DNA-binding assays for five of eight PAX9 mutants; canonical AlphaMissense (> 0.564) showed 8%-21% specificity across both domains. Mechanism did not predict missing teeth, whereas missense variants were milder than null alleles (p = 0.001). AlphaGenome matched SpliceAI and jointly prioritized seven intronic variants.

after.authors: Nakagawa, R.; Yasuhara, Y.; Shimoyama, A.; Nishi, Y.; Kubota, Y.
after.abstract: Objectives: To examine how quickly software vulnerabilities are exploited after public disclosure, and whether hacking breaches at US health care providers changed in size after 2021, a period in which earlier studies had found attacks concentrating on large organizations. Methods: Retrospective analysis of public data. We linked the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog (1,748 entries) with CVE publication dates to measure time to confirmed exploitation by half-year of publication (2021-2025). We also analyzed 8,029 breach reports submitted to the HHS Office for Civil Rights, focusing on hacking/IT incidents at health care providers. Results: Median time to confirmed exploitation was 24 days for vulnerabilities published from late 2021 to mid 2022, 0 days for those published in the second half of 2022, and 6 days in 2023-2025, with no further shortening across 2023-2025 (P = .40). About a quarter were exploited on or before the day of disclosure. Among provider hacking breaches, the share affecting fewer than 5,000 people fell from 42% in 2016 to 32% in 2022 (trend P = .004) and rose to 46% in 2025 (P < .001). Conclusions: The window between disclosure and exploitation had narrowed to about a week before generative AI was widely available. After 2022, breaches moved toward smaller events, reversing the earlier concentration on large organizations. Defenses that depend on patching speed will not protect small providers.

after.authors: Cui, H.; Zhu, Y.; Li, B.; Huang, S.; Xu, T.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Department of Biomedical Engineering, College of Engineering, Shantou University, Shantou, Guangdong, China
after.abstract: Objective/Background: Awakenings after sleep onset are a core measure of sleep continuity, and EEG headbands and closed-loop stimulators, now used at home, must detect each one as it happens, to count it or to stop stimulation. Open sleep stagers match expert scorers, yet have been evaluated only offline over whole nights, so their real-time performance is untested. Patients/Methods: To fill this gap, we developed WakeSentry, which reads only past frontal EEG and learns the moment of waking through an awakening module. We tested it on 1,529 nights from five polysomnography (PSG) cohorts, three clinical, each held out of training, and on 224 headband nights, against GSSC, U-Sleep and YASA. Results: At a matched rate of 0.5 false awakenings per hour, WakeSentry caught more awakenings than GSSC in every cohort and on both headbands. On PSG its sensitivity rose from 63.8% to 70.5%, above U-Sleep and YASA on average. On the headbands it rose from 49.8% to 53.9%, a gain lost without the awakening module. With thresholds preset on the training cohorts, it still outperformed GSSC in six of seven test sets, with at most 0.40 false awakenings per hour. As a replayed stimulator gate, it shortened stimulation during wake in five test sets while staying open for at least 85% of N2 and N3. Conclusions: WakeSentry therefore works in patients and on unseen headbands. It can count awakenings at home and stop stimulation at each one, enabling multi-night monitoring of insomnia and closed-loop stimulation that stops when the sleeper wakes.

after.authors: Alimov, A.; Sharipov, A.; Mamatkulov, B.; Rahimova, S.
after.category: intensive care and critical care medicine
after.abstract: Background: In neonates and young infants, extracorporeal renal r 22 eplacement therapy (RRT) for acute kidney injury (AKI) is often not feasible, and peritoneal dialysis (PD) remains the most practical option. In resource-limited settings, however, dedicated pediatric PD catheters are frequently unavailable. Objective: To evaluate the efficacy and safety of emergency manual PD in critically ill neonates and infants with severe AKI, and to compare complications between adapted nasogastric tubes and Tenckhoff catheters. Methods: In this retrospective cohort study, 28 critically ill children aged 2 days to 3 months (16 boys and 12 girls) received emergency PD between January 2022 and June 2023. Access was obtained with a Tenckhoff catheter in 8 patients (28.6%) and an adapted 12 Fr nasogastric tube in 20 (71.4%). Renal, metabolic, fluid balance and hemodynamic (Vasoactive-Inotropic Score, VIS) parameters were assessed before and during PD. Results: AKI followed cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass in 10 patients (35.7%), sepsis in 12 (42.9%), and congenital pneumonia after complicated delivery in 6 (21.4%). Serum urea, creatinine and potassium decreased significantly (all p < 0.001). Within 72 hours, the daily fluid balance shifted from +42.3 {+/-} 14.8 to -12.4 {+/-} 8.6 mL/kg/day, and the mean VIS fell from 40.4 {+/-} 9.6 to 5.3 {+/-} 3.1 (both p < 0.001). Complication rates did not differ significantly between access types, and no peritonitis occurred. All patients recovered renal function, and there were no deaths. Conclusions: In this small retrospective cohort, emergency manual PD was associated with rapid metabolic correction, reversal of fluid overload and hemodynamic improvement. An adapted nasogastric tube may be a feasible temporary alternative for peritoneal access when Tenckhoff catheters are unavailable; prospective studies are needed to confirm its safety.

after.authors: Dhakal, S.; Kalika, S.
after.abstract: Purpose: The mortality-to-incidence ratio (MIR) from GLOBOCAN is often used to compare cancer outcomes across countries. But in many countries, its two components come from different sources with some estimation methods deriving one from the other. We counted the countries in which both components of MIR are observed, and tested whether correlations between MIR and the Human Development Index (HDI) hold in them. Methods: Using GLOBOCAN 2024 data, we classed a country as having independent MIR when incidence came from cancer registries, mortality was observed, and neither was derived from the other. For each of 37 cancer sites, we calculated the fraction of global new cases occurring in these countries. We compared MIR-HDI Spearman correlations ({rho}) in these countries with the full sample, testing for attenuation beyond range restriction against an HDI-matched null distribution. Results: Only 41 of 186 countries (22%), all with high or very high HDI, had independent MIR. Of the 144 countries with derived MIR, 131 relied on external models. The independent-MIR fraction ranged from 0.12 (Kaposi sarcoma) to 0.77 (thyroid). For 33 of 37 sites, the correlation in independent-MIR countries was within what the narrower HDI range alone would produce. After Benjamini-Hochberg correction, thyroid was the only site whose correlation weakened more than the narrower HDI range would explain ({rho} -0.82 to -0.004, adjusted p = 0.011). Conclusion: No low- or medium-HDI country has independent MIR, and in 131 countries at least one MIR component comes from an external model. Comparing MIR across these countries mostly compares model inputs. In independent-MIR countries, most MIR-HDI associations are consistent with range restriction but for thyroid, the association disappears.

after.abstract: Objectives. To examine associations of kindergarten measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) coverage and vaccination exemptions with state-level measles incidence in the United States, 2024-2026. Methods. In this ecological study of 50 states and Washington, DC (up to 153 jurisdiction-years), we linked CDC surveillance, SchoolVaxView, and Census data. Negative-binomial models estimated incidence rate ratios (IRRs) per percentage-point increase for completed years 2024-2025 (generalized estimating equations) and through MMWR week 39, 2024-2026 (maximum likelihood, adjusted for density and poverty). Results. Cases rose from 269 (2024) to 2,263 (2025); 3,642 were reported provisionally through October 2, 2026. Completed-year IRRs were 0.875 (95% CI=0.806, 0.950) for MMR coverage, 1.202 (1.075, 1.344) for any exemption, and 1.207 (1.059, 1.376) for nonmedical exemption. Adjusted week-39 IRRs were 0.945 (0.837, 1.068), 1.147 (1.004, 1.310), and 1.131 (0.972, 1.316). Under cluster-robust maximum likelihood, completed-year intervals for MMR coverage and nonmedical exemption included 1. Conclusions. Higher exemption prevalence was associated with greater measles incidence; other estimates were imprecise. Public Health Implications. Monitoring exemptions alongside MMR coverage may help identify jurisdictions needing closer vaccination-gap assessment. Ecological findings do not establish causality.

Here, we describe ten years of blood culture surveillance in Agogo, Ghana; the period included a surge in 2017 and a cluster randomised trial of a typhoid conjugate vaccine in 2021-2022. We analysed 20,035 blood cultures from febrile patients enrolled between May 2016 and December 2025 at Asante Akim North, Agogo. after.title: Preprint: Early patient-level quality of care and in-hospital outcomes among preterm and low-birth-weight newborns in Western Kenya: a multicentre retrospective record-review study
after.authors: Shisanya, M. S.; Namusonge, L. N.; Simiyu, C. M.; Kirwa, T. C.; Waswa, P. L.
after.abstract: Preterm and low-birth-weight newborns account for most neonatal deaths in sub-Saharan Africa, and survival depends on the quality and timeliness of care delivered after admission as well as on access to a facility. Quality is usually measured at facility level, and patient-level measures that combine early and later care processes are vulnerable to bias because newborns must survive in order to receive later care. We assessed whether better documented early care was associated with lower in-hospital mortality among preterm and low-birth-weight newborns in eight facilities in Western Kenya. In this multicentre retrospective record review, 291 source newborn records yielded 287 unique records, of which 275 met eligibility criteria and 268 had a calculable early-care patient-level quality score. This study-defined score covered thermal protection, skilled attendance and clinical review, assessment and monitoring, and medicines and fluids, each item scored as not done, partially done or fully done, with not-applicable items excluded from denominators. In-hospital survival status was known for 224 newborns, of whom 57 (25.4%) died before discharge; newborns referred out or still admitted were not counted as survivors. Modified Poisson regression with robust variance estimated risk ratios. Documented early care was high (median 93.5%, interquartile range 83.3-100), while kangaroo mother care was the weakest domain (median 87.5%). Early-care quality was not associated with in-hospital mortality after adjustment for gestational age, multiple pregnancy, birth location, facility and admission severity (adjusted risk ratio 1.03 per 10 percentage points, 95% confidence interval 0.82-1.29), and this null result persisted across nine sensitivity analyses. In contrast, continuing-care quality appeared strongly protective (0.81, 0.74-0.89), a pattern consistent with newborns surviving longer accruing more documented care rather than with a benefit of care itself.

after.authors: Krist, A. H.; Britz, J. B.; Sabo, R. T.; Brooks, E. M.; Niaki, D. S.; Funk, A. J.; Ward, S. A.; Gilbert, J. L.; Webel, B.; Shoen, M.; Lee, J. H.; Burwell, C. A.; Zimmerman, E. H.; Berryhill, J.; Guy, M.; Miller, C.; Labert, J.; Young, M.; Carozza, M.; Topmiller, M.; Chapman, D.; Strayer, S.; DiazGranados, D.; Patrick, N.-S.; Moeller, F. G.
after.abstract: Introduction Health outcomes vary substantially across communities due to multiple factors operating across the socioecological framework. Researchers, health systems, public health and government agencies, and communities often lack integrated data systems that identify communities performing better or worse than expected, characterize factors associated with outcomes, and support action. We propose to develop the Virginia Accountable Health Engagement and Action Dashboard (Va-AHEAD) to identify communities with unexpectedly favorable outcomes (Bright Spots) and the modifiable factors that contribute to their success.   Objectives This protocol describes the design and methodology of a statewide, community-engaged translational science initiative to identify structural factors, community assets, and modifiable drivers associated with population health outcomes using a strengths-based approach. The project aims to co-create community health measures, identify bright spot communities and their assets, support use of findings by researchers and stakeholders, and evaluate impact.   Methods Va-AHEAD integrates person-level and community-level data sources from the Virginia All-Payer Claims Database data, mortality data, census-based measures, and other socioecological datasets. Guided by a coalition of community advisory partners, the project will conduct bright spot analyses and community asset mapping to identify communities performing better than expected and the modifiable community factors that may contribute to their success across 15 priority health topics. Findings will be disseminated through an interactive dashboard, community products, and a statewide learning community. Measures of success include dashboard use, research productivity, care transformation activities, and public health and community action.   Significance Va-AHEAD addresses a critical need for community-informed data systems that move beyond identifying problems to understanding factors associated with success. By integrating advanced analytics, stakeholder engagement, and dissemination strategies, this project will create a scalable model for identifying and spreading effective community approaches to improving health outcomes.

after.authors: Karim, H. T.; Ryan, N. D.; Jones, N. P.; Craske, M.; Eckstrand, K. L.; Price, R. B.; Tripathy, K.; Lenniger, C. J.; Rengasamy, M.; Geramita, M.; Vanderschelden, B.; Diaz, J.; Brodnick, Z.; Dour, H.; Pogue, A.; Medich, C.; Julien, M. M.; Rogers, D.; Forbes, E.
after.abstract: Anhedonia is a hallmark of depression, involves disrupted positive affect (PA), and has been linked to hyperconnectivity between the dorsomedial prefrontal cortex (dmPFC) and nucleus accumbens (NAcc). In previous work, a single session of continuous theta burst stimulation (cTBS) to the dmPFC reduced NAcc-dmPFC functional connectivity (FC), with corresponding improvement in PA. We investigated whether cTBS to dmPFC plus PA-enhancing training is associated with decreased anhedonia, depression, and NAcc-dmPFC FC, and whether FC change corresponds to anhedonia improvement. Fifty youth (15-25 years) with current depression received cTBS (2x/day, 10 days, personalized dmPFC target) plus intersession PA training. Resting-state fMRI and symptom severity were collected pre/post cTBS+PA. In all, 42% of participants responded, and depression, anhedonia, and anxiety improved. Participants with greater decrease in FC experienced more improvement in anhedonia, although NAcc-dmPFC FC remained unchanged on average. Responders exhibited greater improvement than non-responders in anhedonia and anxiety but not FC. Additionally, mutual information modeling revealed that those with greater similarity between the actual target network (based on electrical field modeling) and the intended reward network exhibited a greater decrease in FC. cTBS+PA shows some promise as an intervention for anhedonic depression in youth, with individual differences in FC change relevant to clinical outcomes and precise network targeting a critical issue for modulating the intended network and achieving clinical improvement. Clinicaltrials.gov: NCT05487885

after.authors: Mamaladze, L.; Ormond, C.; Hearn, B.; Chang, Y.-C.; Hassan, A.; Thomson, P. A.; Mathews, C. A.; Byreley, W.; Delisi, L. E.; Heron, E.; Corvin, A.; Ryan, N. M.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Department of Psychiatry, Trinity Translational Medicine Institute, Trinity College Dublin
after.abstract: Although rare non-coding variants are likely involved in psychiatric disorder susceptibility, their contribution is poorly understood. MicroRNAs (miRNAs) regulate gene expression, and targets in the brain include genes involved in neuronal development and synaptic plasticity. Because single-nucleotide variants (SNVs) can alter miRNA processing and target specificity, this can have disproportionate downstream impact on multiple genes affecting pathways that regulate biological processes, making them compelling candidates for mediating psychiatric disorder risk. We investigated rare miRNA variants in whole-genome sequencing (WGS) data from 25 pedigrees with diagnoses including schizophrenia, psychosis, bipolar disorder, depression, OCD, and substance use disorder. Evidence of segregation with schizophrenia and related psychotic disorders was identified for five rare miRNA variants (two seed-region, one mature-region, and two precursor-region variants), including a SNV in the mature-region of miR-4794, segregating strongly in two unrelated pedigrees and identified in a parent-offspring pair with schizophrenia from a third pedigree. One of these two pedigrees also segregates a seed-region SNV in miR-4423-3p, predicted to significantly impact expression-regulation, causing the loss of synaptic gene-targets associated with psychiatric disorders. Collectively, targets of three of the miRNAs are enriched for schizophrenia rare variant risk genes (p-value: 0.00027): six SCHEMA genes were targeted by miR-96 and four genes by miR-4423-3p. While further understanding of miRNA function and validation is required, this study demonstrates the value of integrating structural modelling, target-shift prediction, and pathway enrichment to interpret non-coding variants. This highlights the utility of WGS for identifying and investigating rare non-coding variation in psychiatric disorder susceptibility, supplementing exome-based approaches.

after.authors: Komura, K.; Nagano, M.; Takenaga, R.; Kyan, A.; Inoue, S.; Yamakita, M.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Department of Liberal Arts, Faculty of Agriculture, Meijo University, Aichi, Japan
after.abstract: Background: The parent-reported Sasakawa Sports Foundation Preschoolers' Activity Questionnaire (SSF-PAQ) is from a national survey of Japanese preschoolers' out-of-preschool exercise, active play, screen time, and sleep. We assessed the validity, reliability, measurement error, paper-electronic agreement, and practicality of the Original version and explored a 24-hour version (SSF-PAQ-24). Methods: Children aged 3-6 years from 10 conveniently sampled preschools wore an accelerometer for seven days while parents kept a time-use diary and completed the SSF-PAQ on Days 7 and 10. Criteria were accelerometer-measured physical activity (PA), diary-recorded screen time, and diary- and accelerometer-derived night sleep. Results: The concurrent-validity sample comprised 167 children (Original, 127; SSF-PAQ-24, 40). Original-version correlations were weak for organized PA and active play ({rho} = 0.24) and moderate-to-vigorous PA ({rho} = 0.29) but strong for screen time ({rho} = 0.83) and night sleep ({rho} = 0.78), which averaged 8.2 and 10.7 min/day above the criteria. Test-retest intraclass correlations were 0.78-0.96 for these measures and 0.27-0.89 for setting-specific items. Screen time was higher on paper than electronically. SSF-PAQ-24 activity correlations were not significant ({rho} = 0.17 and 0.06). Completion took 6.5-9.7 minutes. Conclusion: The Original SSF-PAQ's main measures showed good-to-excellent test-retest reliability, and screen time and night sleep correlated strongly with the criteria. Activity-time validity was limited but comparable to that of existing parent-report questionnaires. SSF-PAQ-24 activity items need re-examination in a larger sample.

after.authors: Toujani, S.; Belhaj Hassen, Y.; El Ouni, A.; Belhassen, A.; Abdelkefi, C.; Tekaya, A.; Larbi, T.; Meddeb, Z.; Hamzaoui, S.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Department of Internal Medicine, Mongi Slim Hospital, La Marsa, Tunis
after.abstract: Background. Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) and eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA) are among the rarest systemic vasculitides. They are characterised by variable presentation, necrotising and granulomatous vasculitis, and inconstant ANCA positivity. Objective. We aimed to study the clinical and immunological profile of GPA and EGPA in a Tunisian cohort. Methods. We conducted a descriptive, retrospective, single-centre study over 22 years (2000-2021). GPA and EGPA cases were recorded in an internal medicine department. Diagnosis was based on the ACR 1990 criteria, and/or the 2012 Chapel Hill Consensus Conference, and/or the Diagnostic and Classification Criteria for Vasculitis study (DCVAS 2018). Results. We included 19 GPA and 11 EGPA patients, with median ages of 54 and 52 years, respectively, and a female predominance. Late-onset asthma and hypereosinophilia were constant in EGPA. GPA was predominantly generalised; ANCA specificities were anti-MPO (58%), anti-PR3 (26.5%), dual antigenic specificity (11%) and atypical x-ANCA (5.5%). In EGPA, ANCA were negative (55%) or directed against MPO. ANCA positivity was associated with peripheral neuropathy in EGPA (p=0.013). MPO-ANCA were associated with female sex (p=0.005), and anti-PR3 with male sex (p=0.018), smoking (p=0.019), multiple organ involvement (p=0.006) and gastrointestinal involvement (p=0.033). Under conventional treatment, 36% of EGPA and 42% of GPA patients relapsed. Mortality was 11% in GPA and was associated with a higher BVAS version 3 at diagnosis (p=0.012), heart block (p=0.039) and neurological damage (p=0.050). Conclusion. We provide a detailed profile of GPA and EGPA in a Tunisian cohort. The high prevalence of anti-MPO GPA and the presence of dual positivity suggest a North-South gradient in ANCA specificity and justify larger multicentre studies of the immunological, genetic and environmental determinants of this specificity. Keywords: granulomatosis with polyangiitis; Churg-Strauss syndrome; anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody-associated vasculitis; anti-myeloperoxidase autoantibody; immunology.

after.title: Preprint: Replication of recipient genetic variants associated with survival after lung transplantation
after.authors: Hyvarinen, K.; Partanen, J.; FinnGen,  ; Lauronen, J.; Ritari, J.
after.abstract: Background: Long-term survival after lung transplantation (LTx) remains limited, largely because of chronic lung allograft dysfunction and other post-transplant complications. Genetic studies have suggested recipient single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) to associate with LTx outcomes, but none has been confirmed in independent cohorts. Methods: We evaluated 29 previously published candidate SNPs associated with LTx complications in 201 LTx recipients from FinnGen. Time-to-event analyses were performed for death after transplantation, with censoring at end of follow-up. Each SNP was tested under additive, dominant, and recessive genetic models using Cox proportional hazards regression adjusted for sampling age, sampling year, sex, and the first ten genetic principal components. Replication was defined as nominal association with survival at p < 0.05, surpassing minimum detectable effect at 80% power and concordant direction of effect with the original publication. Results: We found two independent replicated signals: rs4526713-T and rs4149117-T. In multivariable analysis, rs4526713-T and rs4149117-T were associated with increased mortality risk under an additive and dominant models, respectively. A two-SNP score showed a stronger association with mortality than any individual SNP, suggesting an aggregate contribution of replicated genetic risk alleles to post-transplant survival. Conclusions: Our findings support the contribution of host genetic variation to long-term LTx outcomes. However, modest cohort size and use of all-cause mortality rather than allograft dysfunction-specific outcomes require cautious interpretation. Larger donor-recipient genomic studies with harmonized transplant phenotypes are needed before clinical implementation.

after.title: Preprint: Broader functional and memory antibody responses in adult females than males in response to seasonal H3N2 vaccine virus
after.authors: Park, H.-S.; Yin, A.; Parish, M. A.; Hu, J.; Zou, A.; Pandey, R.; Fenstermacher, K. Z. J.; Rothman, R. E.; Pekosz, A.; Toapanta, F. R.; Klein, S.
after.author_corresponding_institution: W. Harry Feinstone Department of Molecular Microbiology and Immunology, Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health
after.abstract: Females of reproductive ages often mount greater antibody responses than males following influenza vaccination, but the breadth and depth of these differences, including antibody-dependent Fc receptor (FcR)-mediated functions have not been explored. Plasma samples were collected from male and female healthcare workers (range of 21-48y; mean of 31y) at 0, 28, and 180 days post-vaccination (DPV) during the 2022-2023 influenza vaccine season to assess antibody responses to A/H1N1, A/H3N2, and B/Victoria vaccine viruses. Females had greater A/H3N2, but not A/H1N1 or B/Victoria, neutralizing antibody (nAb) responses compared to males through 180 DPV, with differences being most pronounced among A/H3N2 responders ([≥]4 fold-change in nAb titers). Memory B cells isolated from female responders secreted more IgG in response to ex vivo H3 stimulation than those from males at 28 and 180 DPV. Before vaccination, female responders had greater anti-H3 IgG responses and Fc{gamma}RIIB (CD32b) antibody binding than males, with females maintaining greater responses through 180 DPV. Female responders had greater H3-specific antibody-dependent monocyte phagocytosis (ADMP) and natural killer cell (ADNK) secretion of IFN{gamma} and CCL4 prior to and after vaccination, with ADMP positively correlating with greater H3N2 neutralization through 180 DPV in females only. Among responders, the durability of ADMP, ADNK, and nAb in females as compared to males defined the sex differences in influenza-vaccine induced immunity. The greater Fc{gamma}R-binding antibodies prior to vaccination in females might improve the durability of both neutralizing and non-neutralizing antibody responses to diverse vaccines, including next generation influenza vaccines.

data.summary: added: Preprint: Shared genetic architecture between digestive infectious diseases and cardiovascular diseases: a genome-wide cross-trait analysis

after.title: Preprint: Shared genetic architecture between digestive infectious diseases and cardiovascular diseases: a genome-wide cross-trait analysis
after.authors: Ni, J.; Pan, J.; Chen, Y.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Department of Cardiology, The Second Affiliated Hospital of Chongqing Medical University
after.abstract: Background Digestive infectious diseases and cardiovascular diseases may share common genetic, inflammatory and immune-related mechanisms. However, the shared genetic architecture between these disease groups, the specific pleiotropic loci involved and the potential contribution of intestinal infectious diseases (IID) to cardiovascular risk remain incompletely understood. Methods We analysed publicly available genome-wide association study summary statistics for 36 binary traits of European ancestry, including 16 digestive infectious disease traits and 20 cardiovascular traits. Univariate linkage disequilibrium score regression was used to estimate SNP-based heritability and prioritise traits. Global and local genetic sharing were evaluated using cross-trait LDSC and SUPERGNOVA. Multi-trait analysis of GWAS, cross-trait sensitivity analyses, FM-summary fine-mapping and Bayesian colocalisation were used to identify and refine pleiotropic loci. Candidate genes and biological functions were investigated using MAGMA, tissue- and cell-type-specific enrichment analyses, transcriptome-wide association analysis and protein-wide association analysis. Bidirectional two-sample Mendelian randomisation and two-step mediation analyses using three independent gut microbiome GWAS resources were subsequently performed. Results Sixteen traits passed heritability quality control, yielding 39 trait pairs with significant global genetic correlations after Bonferroni correction. MTAG identified 41 candidate SNP records and 14 trait-pair-specific lead-SNP records representing eight unique SNPs; 39 candidate records and 12 lead records involved IID. Fine-mapping and colocalisation prioritised eight records representing four unique variants. Locus-based gene prioritisation retained 24 candidate genes across four pairs. Gene-set enrichment identified 43 significant trait-pair-GO term associations, and tissue enrichment identified seven significant associations. Transcriptome-wide analyses implicated 21 candidate genes, and proteome-wide analyses identified four associations involving three proteins. After false discovery rate (FDR) correction, forward MR supported associations of IID liability with cardiac arrhythmias, myocardial infarction, atrial fibrillation and flutter, and ischaemic heart disease; reverse MR supported only cardiac arrhythmias to IID. Five positive exploratory microbiota-IID-cardiovascular mediation patterns were described. Only the Oxalobacter-IID-cardiac arrhythmias indirect effect reached unadjusted P < 0.05. Conclusions Digestive infectious diseases, particularly IID, share substantial genetic architecture with cardiovascular diseases. Integrative genetic analyses identified recurrent pleiotropic loci, candidate genes and putative microbiome-mediated pathways linking IID with cardiovascular outcomes. These findings provide testable hypotheses for further functional validation and clinical investigation.

after.title: Preprint: Lightweight and Explainable AI for Chest Radiograph Classification in Low-Resource Settings: Cross-Dataset Generalization, Grad-CAM Verification, and Uncertainty-Aware Referral
after.authors: Dawood, M.; Bibi, A.
after.abstract: Chest radiography is the most common imaging test worldwide, yet models trained on one hospital's data often fail elsewhere, a critical problem for low-resource hospitals that cannot collect large local datasets. This paper presents a lightweight, explainable framework for chest radiograph classification, trained and evaluated entirely on CPU with public data. EfficientNet-B0 and ResNet-18 are trained on a 10,000-image subset of NIH ChestX-ray14 and evaluated without retraining on a paediatric pneumonia set, alongside a TorchXRayVision DenseNet121 pretrained baseline and a model trained directly on paediatric data. On the NIH test set (n = 2,500), the best single model reaches pneumonia AUC-ROC 0.738 and a two-model ensemble 0.742, while an adult-trained model falls to AUC 0.454 on paediatric images, and, symmetrically, a paediatric-trained model falls to 0.473 on adult NIH images. Pooling the adult and paediatric training sets into one binary pneumonia model changes the picture: a merged EfficientNet-B0 reaches AUC 0.951 (95% CI 0.932-0.967) on paediatric images, the first result whose whole 95% CI clears 0.90, and 0.675 on NIH images with zero sensitivity at threshold 0.5, while a merged ResNet-18 reaches 0.962 on paediatric and 0.606 on NIH images. Pooling fixes the catastrophic cross-domain failure but does not recover adult-only performance, and ensembling a merged model with a single-domain model adds nothing on either test set. Grad-CAM heatmaps are shown for true positives, false negatives and false positives, and Monte Carlo dropout referral raises answered-case accuracy from 0.889 to 0.948 on NIH data but not under domain shift. All results carry bootstrap confidence intervals, and the limits of a 22-positive NIH test set are stated plainly.

after.title: Preprint: Targeted Muscle Reinnervation (TMR) or Regenerative Peripheral Nerve Interface (RPNI) for pain prevention in patients with limb amputation: A systematic review and meta-analysis
after.authors: Gurpegui, D.; del Moral Preciado, J.; Royo, M.; Perez de Rojas, J.; Hontanilla, B.
after.abstract: Background Phantom limb pain (PLP) and residual limb pain (RLP) after amputation impair rehabilitation, prosthetic use, and quality of life. Targeted Muscle Reinnervation (TMR) and Regenerative Peripheral Nerve Interface (RPNI) give transected nerves a physiologic target and may reduce chronic pain. Objective To synthesize evidence on prophylactic TMR and RPNI at amputation for preventing pain. Methods Following PRISMA 2020 and a published protocol (PROSPERO CRD42024617299), seven databases were searched to 31 July 2026 for studies of prophylactic TMR or RPNI at amputation reporting PLP, RLP, symptomatic neuroma, or safety outcomes. Pain intensity (Hedges' g) and incidence (risk ratios, RR) were pooled separately for PLP and RLP using random-effects DerSimonian-Laird models. Risk of bias (ROBINS-I, RoB 2) and certainty (GRADE) were assessed. Results Twenty-seven studies (30 records, 2,154 participants; 16 comparative) were included. In comparative meta-analyses, TMR/RPNI was associated with lower pain intensity and incidence for PLP (g = -0.68, 95% CI -0.82 to -0.55; RR = 0.56, 0.48-0.65) and RLP (g = -0.68, -0.95 to -0.40; RR = 0.55, 0.42-0.73), or about 300 fewer patients with pain per 1,000 treated. Findings were directionally consistent and stable in sensitivity analyses. No study directly compared TMR with RPNI; indirect subgroup analyses showed no difference. Symptomatic neuroma was less frequent but imprecise (4 studies; RR = 0.35, 0.11-1.09); safety outcomes showed no clear differences. No study had low risk of bias; certainty was low to very low. Conclusions Prophylactic TMR and RPNI were associated with consistently less PLP and RLP than standard nerve management, remaining robust in sensitivity analyses excluding serious-risk-of-bias studies or weaker assumptions. Certainty remains low to very low due to observational designs, risk of bias, heterogeneous outcome definitions, and sparse secondary-outcome reporting. Prospective comparative studies with standardized outcomes are needed to compare techniques.

after.title: Preprint: High-resolution spatiotemporal estimates of total and wildfire PM2.5 in the contiguous United States, 2018-2024: Implications for population exposure and mortality burden
after.authors: Liu, N.; Cheong, Y.; Larson, T.; Austin, E.; Seto, E.
after.abstract:
Wildfire smoke has become an increasing public health concern in the contiguous United States (CONUS). Previous studies have provided high-resolution estimates of either total PM2.5 or wildfire-related PM2.5 during the past two decades, but few have focused on the most recent wildfire-intensive years, and jointly estimated both to quantify wildfire contributions to total PM2.5 exposure. This study developed a high-resolution machine learning framework to estimate daily 1-km concentrations of total and wildfire-related PM2.5 across the CONUS from 2018 to 2024. This framework incorporates chemical precursors and wildfire smoke density as predictors and relies on publicly accessible data sources enabling future updates. The model achieved high performance with cross-validated R2 of 0.72 and 0.89 for daily and annual estimates, respectively. Elevated total PM2.5 concentrations were observed along the west coast and in several metropolitan areas across the CONUS. Wildfire smoke contributed substantially to total PM2.5 concentrations during major wildfire years, accounting for approximately 35% of PM2.5 along the west coast in 2020, and over 25% in the eastern U.S. in 2023. Wildfire-related PM2.5 mortality accounted for 20% of PM2.5-attributable deaths along the west coast in 2020 (30 times that in 2019), and 24% in the northeastern U.S. in 2023 (14 times that in 2019). These findings highlight the growing role of wildfire smoke as a major driver of total PM2.5 exposure and associated health risks in both western and eastern U.S., underscoring the need for sustained nationwide public health interventions to reduce wildfire smoke exposure.

after.authors: Hurst, J. H.; Wanchai, V.; Shi, P.; Nookaew, I.; Swain-Lenz, D.; Rowlette, L.-L.; Cleaton, S.; Arnold, J.; Kim, S. Y.; Hite, C.; Kay, K. L.; Catchpole, A.; Kalinova, M.; Killingley, B.; Mann, A.; Wagstaffe, H. R.; Chiu, C.; Kelly, M. S.
after.author_corresponding_institution: University of Arkansas for Medical Sciences
after.abstract: The upper respiratory tract (URT) microbiome modulates the local mucosal immune environment, with potential implications for respiratory viral infection susceptibility and outcomes. We leveraged a first-in-human SARS-CoV-2 challenge study in 34 healthy young adults, 18 of whom became infected, to characterize host gene expression and microbiome composition and dynamics in nasal and throat samples collected before viral inoculation and over the subsequent 14 days. Compared with participants who remained uninfected, participants who became infected had elevated baseline nasal expression of gene modules related to interferon, innate inflammatory, and neutrophil responses, as well as a delayed transcriptional response to viral challenge. Baseline nasal microbiome composition differed modestly by subsequent infection status, with lower relative abundances of Corynebacterium accolens and higher abundances of Dolosigranulum pigrum and Staphylococcus aureus among participants who became infected. Integrated analyses of microbiome and host gene expression data identified coordinated networks of microbiome features and host immune modules that distinguished infected from uninfected participants, including prior to inoculation. Notably, immune modules associated with infection susceptibility were positively correlated with S. aureus abundance and negatively correlated with the abundances of common nasal commensals, Corynebacterium spp. and Staphylococcus epidermidis, linking altered nasal microbiome community structure with the heightened inflammatory state associated with infection susceptibility. Symptom burden and viral load were similarly linked to distinct networks of microbiome and host gene expression features within nasal samples. Taken together, these findings highlight potential microbiome-host interactions within the nasal mucosa that may contribute to differences in respiratory viral infection outcomes.

after.title: Preprint: Rising Tuberculosis Presentations in Ontario, Canada Are Not Explained by Community SARS-CoV-2 Activity: A Population-Based Time-Series Study
after.authors: Wilson, N. J.; Tuite, A.; Lee, C. E.; Berkowitz, R. J.; Wiebe, B.; Hall, J.; Boushy, D.; Fisman, D.
after.abstract:
BackgroundTuberculosis (TB) notifications have increased in several high-income countries since 2020. Proposed explanations include pandemic-related disruption of treatment for latent tuberculosis, changes in population composition, and immune dysfunction following SARS-CoV-2 infection. We assessed whether TB presentations increased during the pandemic era and then tested whether community SARS-CoV-2 activity was followed by increased mycobacterial disease.

MethodsWe conducted a population-based ecological time-series study of first TB- and nontuberculous mycobacterial (NTM)-coded hospital, emergency-department and ambulatory-clinic presentations in the Greater Toronto-Hamilton Area Plus (GTHA+), Ontario (2024 population approximately 11.2 million), from April 2011 through March 2024. NTM served as a comparator because it shares diagnostic pathways with TB but differs epidemiologically. Negative-binomial projection and full-series models estimated pandemic-era changes under three alternative trend assumptions. Distributed lag non-linear models estimated cumulative rate ratios for standardized community viral activity over 0-12 weeks; sensitivity analyses extended the maximum lag to 26 and 52 weeks. Influenza and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) were prespecified comparators; data for five additional viral exposures were obtained after the primary analysis was completed and analysed as exploratory comparisons.

ResultsWe identified 3,985 first TB-coded and 5,214 first NTM-coded acute-care presentations. Across six models, estimated pandemic-era TB increases ranged from 3% to 22%. No model suggested an increased in NTM. SARS-CoV-2 activity was not positively associated with TB (cumulative rate ratio per 1-SD increase over 0-12 weeks 0.909, 95% CI 0.822-1.006) or NTM (0.953, 0.868-1.047). No positive associations were identified in subgroup analyses or with maximum lags of 26 or 52 weeks. Influenza was not associated with either outcome. RSV was associated with TB and NTM; only the RSV-NTM association met the Bonferroni threshold among the prespecified comparisons, and no exploratory associations met the experiment-wide threshold.

ConclusionsWe identified a modest pandemic-era increase in TB-coded acute-care presentations in Ontario, Canada, although its estimated size depended on assumptions about underlying trends. NTM-coded presentations did not increase. Community SARS-CoV-2 activity was not positively associated with subsequent TB or NTM presentations at lags of up to one year and did not provide a temporal explanation for the population-level TB increase. Individual-level effects cannot be excluded.

after.title: Preprint: Human-Agentic AI Collaboration Workflow for Trend Analysis of ChatGPT Applications in Healthcare
after.authors: Chou, P. J.; Lin, Y. H.; Li, E. Y.
after.author_corresponding_institution: National Chung Cheng University, Minhsiung, Chiayi 62130, Taiwan
after.abstract:
BackgroundWith the rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI), large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT have demonstrated strong potential to transform healthcare research and practice. However, LLMs are probabilistic and generate inherently variable outputs, which create risk and uncertainty in healthcare applications. Therefore, analyzing the current research landscape of ChatGPT applications is imperative to understand applied techniques and related concerns and to facilitate their practical integration into healthcare information systems.

ObjectiveLeveraging LLM-based agentic AI with domain experts to analyze trends in ChatGPT healthcare applications and to examine the collaborative and interpretative capacities of LLM agents in broader contexts beyond narrowly defined topics.

MethodsThe review used a systematic search of the PubMed and Web of Science databases, following PRISMA-ScR guidelines, and focused on ChatGPT applications, associated concerns, applied techniques, and usage factors. To support the review process, an adaptive, iterative LLM-based agentic AI with a human-in-the-loop mechanism was employed for automated metadata extraction, identification, classification, and knowledge synthesis. The extracted information was subsequently used for temporal and thematic analyses, citation network construction, and main-path analysis.

ResultsAcross 192 papers, the review identified 511 ChatGPT application types, 690 concern items, and 368 influence usage factors distinct from traditional IT, achieving a metadata error rate of 1.04%. The human-agentic AI workflow enabled efficient synthesis of contextual information across studies, addressing the growing challenge of timely evidence integration in medical knowledge. The findings provide insights into the evolving trajectories of ChatGPT applications in healthcare and demonstrate the value of an expert-validated human-agentic AI workflow in supporting literature analysis and streamlining review processes.

ConclusionThis review provides a comprehensive overview of emerging ChatGPT applications, associated concerns, applied techniques, and usage factors in healthcare. The study further provides meaningful insights into the operational mechanisms of agentic AI, demonstrating the potential of human-AI collaboration for medical informatics research.

after.authors: Walker, D.; Martins, P.; Khaledi, P.; Alexander, H.; Stirling, A.; Neller, M. A.; Kelly, J.; Biggs, V.; Reddiex, H.; Panikkar, A.; Beagley, L.; Flynn, S.; Raju, J.; Voogt, M.; Solomon, M.; Smith, C.; Khanna, R.

after.abstract:
PurposeGlioblastoma (GBM) remains refractory to immunotherapy due to its immunosuppressive microenvironment. Tumour-infiltrating cytomegalovirus (CMV)-specific T cells express elevated programmed cell death protein-1 (PD-1), suggesting checkpoint-mediated dysfunction may limit T-cell therapy. We evaluated the safety and immunological activity of allogeneic CMV-specific T-cell therapy (CYT-101) combined with pembrolizumab.

Patients and MethodsIn this phase I 3+3 dose-escalation study, recurrent GBM patients received four weekly infusions of CYT-101 followed by pembrolizumab. The primary endpoint was safety. Secondary endpoints included progression-free survival at 6 months (PFS-6), overall survival at 6 months (OS-6), and immune correlates of response.

ResultsCYT-101 T-cell therapy demonstrated polyfunctional activity, broad HLA restriction, potent cytolytic function, and diverse T-cell receptor repertoires. Nine patients received study treatment. No dose-limiting toxicities were observed, and the maximum tolerated dose was not reached. Only six adverse events were considered treatment-related, and no treatment-related serious adverse events, graft-versus-host disease, cytokine release syndrome, or neurotoxicity occurred. OS-6 and PFS-6 were 55% and 11%, respectively, with a median overall survival of 9.1 months. No objective clinical responses were seen. Of the nine treated participants, one had stable disease, five had progressive disease, and three were unevaluable by modified RANO criteria. Immune profiling revealed enhanced global CD4+ and CD8+ T-cell function following CYT-101 therapy, while donor-derived CYT-101 clonotypes were detected in six of nine participants, with significant T-cell repertoire remodelling.

ConclusionsAllogeneic CMV-specific T-cell therapy combined with pembrolizumab was safe in recurrent GBM, supporting further evaluation of this strategy to overcome immune dysfunction in GBM.

CYT-101 demonstrated a favourable safety profile without graft-versus-host disease, cytokine release syndrome, neurotoxicity, or treatment-related serious adverse events. Importantly, donor-derived CYT-101 clonotypes were detected following infusion, accompanied by enhanced systemic CD4+ and CD8+ T-cell function and substantial T-cell repertoire remodelling following CYT-101 and pembrolizumab. These findings provide proof-of-concept that allogeneic virus-specific T cells can be safely combined with checkpoint inhibition in GBM, supporting further clinical development and evaluation in larger studies.

after.title: Preprint: High-resolution spatiotemporal estimates of total and wildfire PM2.5 in the contiguous United States, 2018-2024: Implications for population exposure and mortality burden
after.authors: Liu, N.; Cheong, Y.; Larson, T.; Austin, E.; Seto, E.
after.abstract:
Wildfire smoke has become an increasing public health concern in the contiguous United States (CONUS). Previous studies have provided high-resolution estimates of either total PM2.5 or wildfire-related PM2.5 during the past two decades, but few have focused on the most recent wildfire-intensive years, and jointly estimated both to quantify wildfire contributions to total PM2.5 exposure. This study developed a high-resolution machine learning framework to estimate daily 1-km concentrations of total and wildfire-related PM2.5 across the CONUS from 2018 to 2024. This framework incorporates chemical precursors and wildfire smoke density as predictors and relies on publicly accessible data sources enabling future updates. The model achieved high performance with cross-validated R2 of 0.72 and 0.89 for daily and annual estimates, respectively. Elevated total PM2.5 concentrations were observed along the west coast and in several metropolitan areas across the CONUS. Wildfire smoke contributed substantially to total PM2.5 concentrations during major wildfire years, accounting for approximately 35% of PM2.5 along the west coast in 2020, and over 25% in the eastern U.S. in 2023. Wildfire-related PM2.5 mortality accounted for 20% of PM2.5-attributable deaths along the west coast in 2020 (30 times that in 2019), and 24% in the northeastern U.S. in 2023 (14 times that in 2019). These findings highlight the growing role of wildfire smoke as a major driver of total PM2.5 exposure and associated health risks in both western and eastern U.S., underscoring the need for sustained nationwide public health interventions to reduce wildfire smoke exposure.

items.title: Preprint: Patient, carer and clinical stakeholder views on using artificial intelligence and machine learning for the histopathological diagnosis of duodenal biopsies
items.content_text: Objective: Biopsies are examined under the microscope by a pathologist, giving a diagnosis, which guides treatment and predicts prognosis. after.authors: Baby, J. G.; Jaeckle, F.; Williams, J.; Shepherd, K.; Urwin, H.; Soilleux, E. J.
after.abstract:
ObjectiveBiopsies are examined under the microscope by a pathologist, giving a diagnosis, which guides treatment and predicts prognosis. A shortage of pathologists and increasing workload leads to diagnostic delays, while for duodenal (small intestinal) biopsies, variable diagnostic concordance between pathologists limits accuracy. These challenges have motivated us to develop an artificial intelligence (AI)-mediated approach for the automated diagnosis of up to 80% of duodenal biopsies (i.e., most cases of the two most frequent diagnoses: coeliac disease and "normal"). We set out to understand patient, carer and stakeholder views regarding the adoption of such technology.

Methods and AnalysisWe conducted mixed-methods stakeholder engagement (February 2024 to June 2026). We ran a national online patients and carers questionnaire (n=231 respondents) and four UK focus-group workshops, one of which additionally captured Likert-scale attitudes1 immediately before and after a structured educational session (n=34 matched pairs). Healthcare professionals completed an online questionnaire (n=37) and took part in a structured workshop. Quantitative data were summarised descriptively; free-text and workshop data were analysed thematically and triangulated across all sources.

ResultsMost patients and carers supported AI-reliant diagnosis (68.4%) and would strongly trust systems with formal regulatory approval (66.7%). Most wanted to be informed if AI was used (73.6%), but only 52.4% felt explicit permission was necessary. Qualitative themes centred on clear and available evidence of accuracy, human oversight, transparent communication and clear terminology, with the term  machine learning being preferred to  artificial intelligence. Agreement ( agree or  strongly agree combined) with statements relating to trust, acceptance and perceived benefit of AI was significantly higher after a structured educational session (38.2% to 67.6%, 85.3% to 97.1%, and 52.9% to 97.1% respectively; all p[≤]0.003). Healthcare professionals favoured an AI  assistant model over full automation, citing the need for validation, explainability, data governance and workflow integration. Patients also preferred some level of human oversight.

ConclusionPatients and healthcare professionals are cautiously supportive of AI-assisted diagnosis of duodenal biopsies, conditional upon demonstration of accuracy, appropriate human oversight and transparent communication. Attitudes towards AI-assisted diagnosis were more favourable after structured explanation.

{Rightarrow}Attitudes were markedly more favourable after a single structured educational session: agreement that AI could improve duodenal biopsy diagnosis nearly doubled and trust in healthcare AI rose substantially, suggesting that public views of AI in diagnosis can be influenced by clear explanation.

after.title: Preprint: MR-based normative volumetric analyses reveal genotype-dependent brain anomalies in FGFR-related craniosynostoses
after.authors: Delassus, O.; Sadoine, J.; Paternoster, G.; Chollet, L.; Ndambidi Yungi, B.; Beaufort, Q.; Taverne, M.; Boddaert, N.; Mangin, J.-F.; Khonsari, R. H.; Germanaud, D.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Universite Paris-Saclay, CEA, Joliot Institute, NeuroSpin, UNIACT
after.abstract: Craniostenosis, a cranial malformation due to premature suture fusion, includes rare FGFR-related conditions such as Crouzon (CS), Muenke (MS), and Apert (AS) syndromes. These mutations affect skull but also brain development and are associated with variable neurodevelopmental outcomes. This brain impairment is still poorly described and understood, prompting for neuroimaging anatomical studies. We thus investigated regional brain growth and volumetric scaling in patients with these three syndromes and non-syndromic non-FGFR-related craniostenoses, using a normative modelling framework. We analyzed a rare set of brain MRI from 65 patients close to first cranial surgery time (30 CS among which 23 pre-surgery, 4 AS, 6 MS, 23 non-syndromic) and 130 typically developing controls. Millimetric 3D T1-weighted images were segmented into 6 cortical and 3 subcortical regions (AssemblyNet, Morphologist). After harmonization (ComBat), normative growth curves (Turner model) and static scaling curves (power-law model, effect of brain size regardless of age) were derived in controls. Patient deviations were assessed using permutation tests on mean normalized distance to typical model and abnormality rates (10th/90th percentiles). Patients with CS showed typical brain volumes for age except for enlarged ventricles, but slightly overscaled frontal volumes for brain size. Non-syndromic patients showed very similar volume distribution for age and brain size than CS ones. Patients with AS displayed increased total brain, temporal, cerebellar and central volumes for age, with overscaled temporal and cerebellar regions but underscaled frontal volumes for brain size. Patients with MS showed a similar, though milder, pattern: increased temporal volume for age, with temporal overscaling but frontal underscaling for frain size. Our findings reveal genotype-dependent brain anomalies in FGFR-related craniosynostoses, with a convergent pattern of temporal-frontal disproportions in AS and MS, associated with very specific mutations in the FGFR2 and 3 genes respectively, contrasting with a much more typical brain organization in more heterogeneous CS and non-syndromic patients. Beyond the pathophysiological meaning of these results, which call for a larger similar study covering as wide a range of patient variability as possible, our work highlights the relevance of normative modelling approach for characterizing rare craniofacial disorders using clinical MRI datasets.

after.title: Preprint: Wavelet-derived indices of cardiac vagal and vasomotor oscillations as a new tool to better understand autonomic imbalance in post-COVID-19 dysautonomia
after.authors: Romero Fragoso, I.; Sainz-Jimenez, A.; Reyes Cruz, T.; Chiquete, E.; Tamez-Torres, K.; Sifuentes-Osornio, J.; Fossion, R.; Estanol, B.; Aceves-Buendia, J. d. J.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Instituto Nacional de Ciencias Medicas y Nutricion Salvador Zubiran
after.abstract:
BackgroundWhen aiming to quantify autonomic imbalance, conventional heart rate variability (HRV) analysis generally reduces each posture to a single spectral value derived from interbeat intervals (IBI) alone. This analysis based only in IBI obscures transient events during blood pressure changes. We propose two wavelet-derived indices that quantify cardiac vagal and vasomotor sympathetic oscillations separately and over time. Since autonomic imbalance is directly related to baroreflex sensitivity (BRS), we evaluated them against an estimate of baroreflex sensitivity in post-COVID-19 patients.

MethodsIn this study, 121 participants (32 healthy controls and 89 patients with persistent post-COVID-19 autonomic symptoms) underwent an active standing test with continuous finger blood pressure. The continuous wavelet transform with generalized Morse wavelets yielded time-varying high-frequency power of IBI and low-frequency power of systolic blood pressure (SBP). Two new indices were proposed: Index I combined the magnitude and variability of HF IBI power (aimed to quantify parasympathetic activity), and the index J combined LF SBP power with the rate of its transient elevations (bursts), which aims to quantify sympathetic vasomotor activity; J/I was their ratio. Indices were computed for supine and orthostatic periods and compared with conventional HRV and BRS measurements.

ResultsIndex I correlated strongly with HF power of IBI and was lower in all patient subgroups than in controls, Index J had only a weak relation with LF power of IBI. On standing, J increased most in the subgroups with the worst baroreflex function. Orthostatic J/I was higher than in controls amongst patients, while LF/HF showed no differences. J/I was inversely correlated with BRS, most strongly when standing, and more strongly than LF/HF also. Adding J to I raised the cross-validated variance explained in orthostatic BRS substantially. In one example patient, a window during symptoms showed vasomotor oscillations that were hidden in the posture average.

ConclusionsWavelet-derived indices from routine beat-to-beat recordings separate cardiac vagal modulation from sympathetic vasomotor oscillations and their transients. J/I correlates with BRS impairment more closely than LF/HF, providing a potential alternative estimate of autonomic balance, and its time-resolved visual output allows analysis of clinically relevant windows within a posture. The new proposed variables allowed an evaluation of autonomic imbalance that could be applied to different pathologies.

after.title: Preprint: High-resolution spatiotemporal estimates of total and wildfire PM2.5 in the contiguous United States, 2018-2024: Implications for population exposure and mortality burden
after.authors: Liu, N.; Cheong, Y.; Larson, T.; Austin, E.; Seto, E.
after.abstract:
Wildfire smoke has become an increasing public health concern in the contiguous United States (CONUS). Previous studies have provided high-resolution estimates of either total PM2.5 or wildfire-related PM2.5 during the past two decades, but few have focused on the most recent wildfire-intensive years, and jointly estimated both to quantify wildfire contributions to total PM2.5 exposure. This study developed a high-resolution machine learning framework to estimate daily 1-km concentrations of total and wildfire-related PM2.5 across the CONUS from 2018 to 2024. This framework incorporates chemical precursors and wildfire smoke density as predictors and relies on publicly accessible data sources enabling future updates. The model achieved high performance with cross-validated R2 of 0.72 and 0.89 for daily and annual estimates, respectively. Elevated total PM2.5 concentrations were observed along the west coast and in several metropolitan areas across the CONUS. Wildfire smoke contributed substantially to total PM2.5 concentrations during major wildfire years, accounting for approximately 35% of PM2.5 along the west coast in 2020, and over 25% in the eastern U.S. in 2023. Wildfire-related PM2.5 mortality accounted for 20% of PM2.5-attributable deaths along the west coast in 2020 (30 times that in 2019), and 24% in the northeastern U.S. in 2023 (14 times that in 2019). These findings highlight the growing role of wildfire smoke as a major driver of total PM2.5 exposure and associated health risks in both western and eastern U.S., underscoring the need for sustained nationwide public health interventions to reduce wildfire smoke exposure.

after.authors: Wang, W.; Olsman, R.; Grashof, D. G. B.; Scheffers, L.; Leenders, M.; Robbrecht, D. G. J.; Snaebjornsson, P.; Katsikis, P. D.; van de Wouw, Y. A. J.; van de Werken, H. J. G.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Department of Immunology, Erasmus MC, University Medical Center Rotterdam, Rotterdam, the Netherlands
after.abstract:
BackgroundCancer of unknown primary (CUP) is a metastatic, heterogeneous malignancy accounting for 2-5% of cancer diagnoses globally. Failure to identify the primary site precludes tumor-type-specific therapy and, together with an aggressive clinical course, contributes to poor survival. The biological mechanisms driving these behaviors remain poorly understood. A deeper understanding of CUP biology is therefore essential to improve diagnostic precision and therapeutic strategies. To address this knowledge gap, we comprehensively characterized the multi-omics landscape of CUP and identified biological and potentially therapeutic targets beyond tissue-of-origin (ToO) assignment.

MethodsWhole-genome sequencing (WGS) data from 283 CUP patients were analyzed for ToO predictions, mutational signatures, driver alterations, genetic immune escape (GIE), and clinically actionable alterations. Matched RNA-sequencing (RNA-seq) data from 79 cases were used to characterize functional gene expression signatures and define transcriptomic subtypes. Clinical, WGS, and RNA-seq data were integrated via weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA).

ResultsHigh-confidence ToO predictions (likelihood >80%) were obtained for 58% of CUPs, most commonly predicting lung, gastrointestinal, and biliary tract origins. Mutational signatures clustering revealed four subgroups dominated by tobacco smoking, defective DNA mismatch repair (dMMR), UV exposure, and APOBEC activity, while a fifth group, comprising most tumors (n=169; 60%), showed mixed mutational processes. The cohort also frequently exhibited mutations in established cancer driver genes, including TP53, CDKN2A, KRAS, and epigenetic modifiers ARID1A, SMARCA4, and ARID2. GIE alterations occurred in 35% of tumors, mostly involving HLA-I genes. Transcriptomic profiling defined five subtypes with different degrees of immune infiltration, fibrosis, and tumor proliferation. These subtypes were not significantly associated with clinical or genomic features, indicating that the tumor microenvironment (TME) represents another layer of CUP heterogeneity. WGCNA further linked proliferative programs to cell-cycle, DNA-replication, and neuroendocrine features. WGS data identified potentially targetable alterations in 64% of the CUP patients.

ConclusionsCUP comprises biologically heterogeneous tumors with diverse predicted origins, mutational histories, and TME subtypes. Transcriptomic profiling and integrated genomics suggest that immune escape and rapid proliferation contribute to the clinical aggressive behavior. Together, these findings provide a molecular framework for understanding CUP heterogeneity and support therapeutic stratification by both ToO predictions and tumor-specific molecular alterations.
